summary:
Same-sex relations are legal in Liechtenstein and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited, but gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are not covered by any anti-discrimination statute in force. No procedure exists for changing a legal gender marker, and no law restricts access to sex-segregated facilities. A visitor entering for a short stay therefore faces no legal exposure from these gaps, which bind residents, employers and public bodies rather than travellers.

Entry falls under the common border-free travel zone operated with Switzerland and Austria, and no source reports friction at that border for trans travellers. There is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence in the country. Liechtenstein is very small, has very low crime, and is closely integrated with both neighbouring states.

Civil marriage and joint adoption have been available to same-sex couples since January 2025. The legislative route ran through registered partnerships, which members of the Landtag described in a September 2022 motion as a second-class marriage, and the motion sought to open civil marriage regardless of gender and sexual orientation and to remove the remaining legal differences.

Official statements from the highest level of the state have cut the other way. In his New Year interview of January 2016, Prince Hans-Adam II called rainbow families irresponsible, said children have a right to a normal family, and suggested that Liechtenstein could ignore an adverse ruling of the European Court of Human Rights. The local LGBT organisation Flay said it was shocked, and the Freie Liste called the remarks contrary to the Constitution and the Convention. In 2021 the Prince said he had nothing against marriage equality except adoption. The state religion is Roman Catholicism, and the Archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality.

Social attitudinal evidence is thin but describes a quiet environment rather than an organised hostile one. A 2012 profile found no organised gay scene at a population of about 35,000, since friendship networks serve that function, and reported few organised enemies: no religious extremists, no right-wing skinheads, no political figures demanding homophobic laws, with gay people living comfortably and with little interference. The first Pride was held in 2022. Intercultural genital mutilation is not prohibited by law.
tangentialFactors:
Official hostility in Liechtenstein has come from the throne and the pulpit rather than from statute. The Prince's 2016 remarks on rainbow families and on the authority of the European Court of Human Rights, and the Archbishop's public opposition to marriage equality, indicate elite-level disapproval that has not translated into restrictive legislation.

The direction of travel is toward legal equality: registered partnerships were opened first, then civil marriage and joint adoption in January 2025, with a Landtag motion in September 2022 pressing to close the remaining gaps. The 2016 and 2021 statements by the Prince predate that settlement.

Liechtenstein's position is comparable to that of other very small European states, a group that a Reuters feature examined as catching up on LGBT equality; that page was not retrievable at research time. The 2012 attitudinal account is dated by more than a decade and predates the first Pride in 2022 and the 2025 marriage reform, so it evidences the social environment of that period rather than the present one.
localsOnly:
Residents have no legal route to change a gender marker on identity documents, which affects employment, health and administrative dealings rather than visitors passing through.

Gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are absent from every anti-discrimination statute in force, so residents who face discrimination on those grounds have no statutory claim, while discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited.

Intercultural genital mutilation is not prohibited by law.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry and adopt jointly since January 2025, ending the arrangement under which registered partnerships were regarded in the Landtag as a second-class marriage.

The state religion is Roman Catholicism, and the Archbishop publicly opposed marriage equality. The first Pride took place in 2022, and at a population of about 35,000 there is no organised scene, only friendship networks.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses access to sex-segregated facilities, airport or border screening of trans travellers, or access to gender-affirming medical care; the statements that no facilities statute exists and that there is no documented anti-trans violence rest on the absence of reporting rather than on an affirmative survey.

The Reuters feature on small European states and LGBT equality returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be read, so its claims are not carried here.

The outlying claim about intercultural genital mutilation not being prohibited is drawn from a single country overview and is not corroborated by a statute or a second source.

The 2012 attitudinal account is more than a decade old and predate the 2022 Pride and the 2025 marriage reform; it is unresolved whether its description of a tolerant social environment still holds.
